crystal-001.question: In a face-centered cubic (FCC) metal, how many atoms touch a given atom at the nearest-neighbor distance (the coordination number)?
crystal-001.explanation: In FCC, each atom touches 6 atoms within its own {111} plane and 3 atoms in each of the {111} planes above and below, so the coordination number is 12. This is the maximum possible for packing spheres of equal size, and HCP also has 12. Eight is the coordination number of BCC (the body-center atom touches the 8 corner atoms of the cube), and 6 is that of simple cubic (SC). Structures with larger coordination numbers also have higher packing factors: about 0.52 for SC, about 0.68 for BCC, and about 0.74 for FCC and HCP. Cu, Al, Ni, Au and γ-iron are typical FCC examples.

crystal-002.question: What is the net number of atoms in a body-centered cubic (BCC) unit cell?
crystal-002.explanation: Each corner atom is shared by 8 unit cells, so it contributes 1/8, while the body-center atom belongs entirely to that cell. The net number of atoms is therefore 8 × 1/8 + 1 = 2. Nine comes from counting each corner atom as a whole atom without considering sharing, and 4 is the value for FCC (corners 8 × 1/8 + face centers 6 × 1/2 = 4). The number of atoms per unit cell n goes straight into the density calculation ρ = nM/(N_A a³), so you need to know it reliably for each structure. SC has 1, and the hexagonal-prism cell of HCP has 6.

crystal-003.question: Treating atoms as hard spheres of equal size, what is the atomic packing factor of the FCC structure (the fraction of the unit-cell volume occupied by atoms)?
crystal-003.explanation: In FCC, atoms touch along the face diagonal, so √2a = 4r, that is, a = 2√2r. With 4 atoms per unit cell, the packing factor is 4 × (4/3)πr³ / (2√2r)³ = π/(3√2) ≈ 0.74. About 0.68 is the BCC value (atoms touch along the body diagonal, a = 4r/√3, 2 atoms), and about 0.52 is the SC value (a = 2r, 1 atom, π/6). HCP with the ideal c/a also reaches 0.74 and is the other close-packed structure alongside FCC. The size of each interstitial site, however, runs the other way: it is smaller in the less densely packed BCC (the largest sphere fitting an octahedral site has a radius of about 0.41r in FCC but about 0.15r in BCC), because BCC divides its larger total free volume into many small sites.

crystal-004.question: Which correctly relates the lattice parameter a and the atomic radius r in the BCC structure? Assume hard-sphere atoms with nearest neighbors in contact.
crystal-004.explanation: In BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal that joins a corner atom to the body-center atom. The body diagonal has length √3a and spans four atomic radii, so √3a = 4r, that is, a = 4r/√3 ≈ 2.31r. a = 2√2r is the FCC relation (contact along the face diagonal, √2a = 4r), and a = 2r is the SC relation (contact along the cube edge). If you overlook the fact that BCC atoms do not touch along the face diagonal, it is easy to apply the FCC relation by mistake.

crystal-005.question: Copper has the FCC structure with a lattice parameter of 0.3615 nm and a molar mass of 63.55 g/mol. Taking Avogadro's number as 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹, which value is closest to the calculated density of copper?
crystal-005.explanation: The density is ρ = nM/(N_A a³), and the FCC unit cell contains n = 4 atoms. With a = 0.3615 nm = 3.615×10⁻⁸ cm, a³ ≈ 4.724×10⁻²³ cm³, so ρ = 4 × 63.55 / (6.022×10²³ × 4.724×10⁻²³) ≈ 8.94 g/cm³, in good agreement with the measured value of about 8.96 g/cm³. About 2.23 g/cm³ is calculated with n = 1 (treating it as SC), and about 4.47 g/cm³ with n = 2 (treating it as BCC). The conversion from nm to cm (1 nm = 10⁻⁷ cm) is also a common slip, so make the units consistent before cubing.

crystal-006.question: If the lattice parameter of α-iron (BCC) is 0.2866 nm, which value is closest to the atomic radius in the hard-sphere model?
crystal-006.explanation: In BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal, so √3a = 4r gives r = √3a/4 = 1.732 × 0.2866/4 ≈ 0.124 nm. About 0.101 nm comes from applying the FCC relation r = √2a/4, and about 0.143 nm from applying the simple cubic relation r = a/2. FCC γ-iron has a larger lattice parameter of about 0.36 nm, but its atomic radius differs by only a few percent; most of the difference in lattice parameter comes from the difference in atomic arrangement (structure).

crystal-007.question: In a cubic crystal, a plane intercepts the x axis at 1a and the y axis at 2a, and is parallel to the z axis. What are its Miller indices?
crystal-007.explanation: Miller indices are found by expressing the intercepts on each axis in units of the lattice parameter, taking their reciprocals and reducing to the smallest integer ratio. The intercepts are 1, 2 and ∞, so the reciprocals are 1, 1/2 and 0; multiplying by 2 gives (210). (120) is the mistake of listing the intercepts 1 and 2 without taking reciprocals. A plane parallel to the z axis has an infinite z intercept, so l = 0 always, and (102), whose third index is not zero, is also wrong. If the plane passes through the origin, move the origin to a neighboring lattice point before reading the intercepts.

crystal-008.question: Which correctly pairs the close-packed planes and close-packed directions of an FCC metal?
crystal-008.explanation: In FCC, the {111} planes are the most densely packed, and within them atoms touch along the face diagonals, the <110> directions. Slip in FCC metals occurs on {111}<110>; there are 4 kinds of {111} plane, each with 3 <110> directions, giving 12 slip systems. {110} planes and <111> directions are the densest plane and direction in BCC, a pairing that is easily confused with FCC. {100} planes and <100> directions are the densest plane and direction in SC and are not close-packed in FCC.

crystal-009.question: Which value is closest to the interplanar spacing of the (111) planes of aluminum (FCC, lattice parameter 0.405 nm)?
crystal-009.explanation: The interplanar spacing in a cubic crystal is d = a/√(h² + k² + l²), so for (111), d = 0.405/√3 ≈ 0.234 nm. About 0.135 nm is the mistake of taking a/3 without the square root, and about 0.701 nm is the mistake of multiplying a by √3, which gives the length of the body diagonal. The spacing gets smaller as the indices get larger, and in XRD, planes with smaller d diffract at higher angles. This formula applies only to cubic crystals; tetragonal and hexagonal crystals need formulas that treat the lattice parameters a and c separately.

crystal-010.question: Which statement about the ideal hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure is correct?
choices: c/a ≈ 1.633, and its packing factor is about 0.74, the same as FCC
c/a ≈ 1.633, and its packing factor is about 0.68, the same as BCC
c/a ≈ 1.414, and its packing factor is about 0.74, the same as FCC
crystal-010.explanation: HCP stacks close-packed planes in an ABAB… sequence, and when hard spheres touch ideally, c/a = √(8/3) ≈ 1.633. The coordination number is 12 and the packing factor is about 0.74, the same close packing as FCC, which stacks ABCABC…. About 0.68 is the packing factor of BCC, and 1.414 (√2) is the ratio of the face diagonal to the edge in FCC, not the c/a of HCP. Real HCP metals deviate from the ideal c/a: about 1.62 for Mg, about 1.59 for Ti and about 1.86 for Zn. Because they have few slip systems, HCP metals tend to be less ductile at room temperature than FCC metals.

crystal-011.question: In a cubic crystal, which value is closest to the angle between the [100] and [111] directions?
crystal-011.explanation: In cubic crystals, the angle between two directions can be found from the dot product. For [100] and [111], cosθ = (1×1 + 0×1 + 0×1)/(1 × √3) = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577, so θ ≈ 54.7°. About 35.3° is the angle between [110] and [111] (cosθ = 2/√6), and about 45.0° is the angle between [100] and [110]. Because the [hkl] direction is normal to the (hkl) plane in cubic crystals, 54.7° is also the angle between the (100) and (111) planes, familiar as the slope of the {111} sidewalls that appear when (100) silicon is etched in an alkaline solution.

crystal-012.question: At 912 °C, pure iron transforms from BCC α-iron (lattice parameter 0.2904 nm) to FCC γ-iron (lattice parameter 0.3647 nm). Which correctly describes the change in volume per atom? Both lattice parameters are values at 912 °C.
crystal-012.explanation: The volume per atom is the unit-cell volume divided by the number of atoms in the cell. For BCC it is 0.2904³/2 ≈ 0.01225 nm³, and for FCC 0.3647³/4 ≈ 0.01213 nm³, so the change is about −0.97%: a contraction of about 1%. The volume decreases because the structure becomes the more densely packed FCC; calling it an expansion is a sign error. Doubling comes from comparing unit-cell volumes directly (0.3647³/0.2904³ ≈ 1.98), overlooking that the BCC cell holds 2 atoms and the FCC cell 4. This volume change can be observed as a transformation point in dilatometry.

crystal-013.question: Which gives the correct numbers of octahedral and tetrahedral interstitial sites in an FCC unit cell?
crystal-013.explanation: The octahedral sites in FCC lie at the body center of the unit cell (1 site) and at the midpoints of its 12 edges. Each edge midpoint is shared by 4 unit cells, giving 12 × 1/4 = 3, for a total of 4. The tetrahedral sites lie at the centers of the 8 small cubes obtained by dividing the unit cell into eighths; all are inside the cell, so there are 8. Since the FCC cell contains 4 atoms, there are 1 octahedral site and 2 tetrahedral sites per atom. Counting only the body-center site as octahedral overlooks the edge midpoints. The combination with the two numbers swapped is also wrong. In the NaCl structure, Na⁺ fills all the octahedral sites of the FCC array of Cl⁻; in zinc blende, Zn²⁺ fills half of the tetrahedral sites.

crystal-014.question: A plane in a hexagonal crystal is described by four indices (hkil) (Miller-Bravais indices) using three basal axes a₁, a₂, a₃ and the c axis. Which relation correctly gives the index i from h and k?
crystal-014.explanation: The three basal axes a₁, a₂, a₃ of a hexagonal crystal make 120° with one another, so they are not independent: a₃ = −(a₁ + a₂). The plane indices are therefore not independent either, and h + k + i = 0, that is, i = −(h + k). For example, one prism plane has h = 1, k = 0, i = −1, l = 0, and the basal plane has h = k = i = 0, l = 1. The extra index i is added so that planes made equivalent by the sixfold symmetry are expressed by permutations of the same numbers; with three indices (hkl), equivalent planes end up with dissimilar-looking indices. Neither i = h + k nor i = h − k satisfies the requirement that the three basal indices sum to zero.

crystal-015.question: Which is closest to the planar density (number of atoms per unit area) of the (111) plane of copper (FCC, lattice constant 0.3615 nm)?
crystal-015.explanation: The (111) plane cuts the unit cell in an equilateral triangle whose side is the face diagonal √2a, with area (√3/4)(√2a)² = (√3/2)a². The triangle contains 3 corner atoms at 1/6 each and 3 edge-midpoint atoms at 1/2 each, 2 atoms in total. The planar density is therefore 2/((√3/2)a²) = 4/(√3a²) = 4/(1.732 × 0.3615²) ≈ 17.7 nm⁻². About 15.3 nm⁻² is the (100) value 2/a², which shows that the (111) plane is more densely packed. About 8.8 nm⁻² counts only 1 atom in the triangle. The {111} planes, with the highest planar density, are the slip planes of FCC and also have the largest interplanar spacing.

crystal-016.question: Of the 7 crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices, the tetragonal system has only the simple tetragonal and body-centered tetragonal lattices; no "base-centered tetragonal" lattice is counted. Which is the correct reason?
choices: Taking half of each base diagonal as a new axis turns a base-centered tetragonal lattice into a smaller simple tetragonal lattice
Redefining the axes turns a base-centered tetragonal lattice into the body-centered tetragonal lattice, so it would be counted twice
Placing a lattice point at the center of the base destroys the fourfold rotation axis, so tetragonal symmetry is lost
crystal-016.explanation: The base of a base-centered tetragonal cell is a square of side a with lattice points at its corners and at its center. Taking half of each base diagonal as a new axis gives a square of side a/√2 with lattice points only at its corners, so the same lattice can be described as a simple tetragonal lattice with half the cell volume. It is therefore not an independent Bravais lattice. It is the face-centered tetragonal lattice, not the base-centered one, that becomes body-centered tetragonal when the axes are redefined. Adding a point at the center of a square also keeps the fourfold rotation axis, so the claim that the symmetry is lost is wrong too.

crystal-017.question: In a cubic crystal, which direction lies in (is parallel to) the (110) plane?
crystal-017.explanation: In a cubic crystal the [hkl] direction is the normal of the (hkl) plane, so a direction [uvw] lies in the plane when its dot product with the normal is zero: hu + kv + lw = 0 (the zone law). For [001], 1×0 + 1×0 + 0×1 = 0, so it lies in the (110) plane. For [110] the dot product is 1 + 1 + 0 = 2; it is the normal of the (110) plane itself. [111] also gives 2 and does not lie in the plane. In the BCC slip systems {110}<111>, [111] lies in the {110} planes for which the dot product is zero, such as the plane with h = −1, k = 1, l = 0. A <111> direction does not lie in every {110} plane.

crystal-018.question: The diamond structure (the structure of Si and Ge) places two atoms at each FCC lattice point, so the unit cell contains 8 atoms, and nearest neighbors touch at one quarter of the body diagonal, √3a/4. Treating the atoms as hard spheres, which is closest to the atomic packing factor?
crystal-018.explanation: Nearest neighbors touch, so √3a/4 = 2r, that is, a = 8r/√3. The packing factor is 8 × (4/3)πr³ / (8r/√3)³ = π√3/16 ≈ 0.34. About 0.17 counts only 4 atoms in the cell, as in FCC, and about 0.74 simply applies the FCC packing factor. In the diamond structure each atom forms covalent bonds with 4 neighbors in tetrahedral directions, so the coordination number is only 4 and the structure is quite open. With directional covalent bonds, the bond angles take priority over packing spheres densely.

crystal-019.question: The Young's modulus of a single crystal of iron differs strongly with direction: about 273 GPa along [111] and about 125 GPa along [100]. Yet an ordinary polycrystalline iron bar has a Young's modulus of about 210 GPa in practically every direction. What is the main reason?
choices: The grain orientations are random, so the directional differences of many grains average out
The grain boundaries carry most of the elastic deformation, so the effect of crystal orientation does not show
In a polycrystal the interatomic bonds become equally strong in all directions, so the crystal itself becomes isotropic
crystal-019.explanation: The elastic modulus of a single crystal is anisotropic because the atomic arrangement differs with direction. In a polycrystal each grain is still anisotropic, but the grain orientations are random, so averaging over many grains gives nearly the same value in every direction. Grain boundaries occupy only a tiny fraction of the volume and do not carry most of the deformation. The bonding inside each grain is the same as in a single crystal, so the crystal itself does not become isotropic. When the grains have a preferred orientation (a texture), as in rolled sheet, a polycrystal also shows anisotropy in its modulus and plastic behavior.

crystal-020.question: For magnesium (HCP, a = 0.321 nm, c = 0.521 nm), which is closest to the interplanar spacing of the plane with Miller-Bravais indices h = 1, k = 0, i = −1, l = 1 (one of the pyramidal planes)? Use 1/d² = (4/3)(h² + hk + k²)/a² + l²/c² for hexagonal crystals.
crystal-020.explanation: With h = 1 and k = 0, h² + hk + k² = 1, so 1/d² = (4/3)/0.321² + 1/0.521² ≈ 12.94 + 3.68 = 16.62 nm⁻², giving d ≈ 0.245 nm. About 0.227 nm applies the cubic formula d = a/√(h² + k² + l²) to the three indices (101), giving a/√2; about 0.273 nm drops the factor 4/3. The basal axes of a hexagonal crystal are at 120° to one another, so the cubic formula does not apply. In XRD with Cu Kα radiation (0.15406 nm), the reflection from this plane appears at 2θ ≈ 36.6°.

crystal-021.question: A crystal has unit-cell edges with a = b ≠ c, and all three angles between the axes are 90°. To which crystal system does it belong?
crystal-021.explanation: The tetragonal system is a cube stretched or compressed along one axis only, with a = b ≠ c and α = β = γ = 90°. Examples are martensite in quenched steel (body-centered tetragonal) and BaTiO₃ at room temperature. Three unequal edges with all angles at 90° define the orthorhombic system. The hexagonal system also has a = b ≠ c, but the angle between the a and b axes is 120°, with the other two at 90°. Looking only at edge lengths leads to confusing tetragonal and hexagonal. The seven crystal systems are distinguished by combinations of edge lengths and axial angles (ultimately by symmetry); the cubic system has a = b = c with all angles at 90°.

crystal-022.question: Which statement correctly describes the FCC structure viewed as a stacking of close-packed layers of atoms?
choices: The close-packed layers are the {111} planes normal to the cube body diagonal ([111] direction), stacked ABCABC… with a three-layer period
The close-packed layers are the {100} planes normal to a cube face ([100] direction), stacked ABAB… with a two-layer period
The close-packed layers are the {111} planes normal to the cube body diagonal ([111] direction), stacked ABAB… with a two-layer period
crystal-022.explanation: Packing equal spheres as densely as possible in a plane gives a layer (A) in which each sphere touches six others. The next layer sits in one set of hollows (B), and the third layer can go in two ways. When the third layer sits in positions (C) different from both A and B, giving ABCABC… with a three-layer period, the result is FCC, and these close-packed layers are the {111} planes normal to the body diagonal of the unit cell. ABAB… stacking with a two-layer period is HCP, whose close-packed layer is the basal plane normal to the c axis. The {100} planes of FCC are not close-packed. This picture also shows clearly that a single error in the FCC stacking sequence creates a stacking fault with a locally HCP-like arrangement.

crystal-023.question: The hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure does not correspond directly to any of the 14 Bravais lattices. Which description of HCP is correct?
choices: Every atom can be treated as a lattice point, giving a separate lattice, base-centered hexagonal, with points also at the basal-face centers
It is a simple hexagonal lattice with a pair of atoms placed at each lattice point; the atoms of the middle layer are not lattice points
It is an FCC unit cell stretched along the c axis, so as a lattice it is the same as body-centered tetragonal
crystal-023.explanation: Lattice points are a set of points each of which has exactly the same surroundings. In HCP, the atoms of the basal layer and those of the middle layer have their neighbors arranged in different orientations, and no pure translation maps one onto the other. The middle-layer atoms therefore cannot be lattice points, and HCP is described as a simple hexagonal lattice with a pair of atoms, at (0, 0, 0) and (2/3, 1/3, 1/2), placed at each lattice point. Treating every atom as a lattice point violates the definition of a lattice point, and there is no Bravais lattice called base-centered hexagonal. HCP also differs from FCC in the stacking sequence of close-packed layers; it is not a stretched FCC or a tetragonal lattice.

crystal-024.question: Which statement about the rotational symmetries that a crystal with translational periodicity can have is correct?
choices: All 1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, 5- and 6-fold rotation axes are allowed, and crystals with 5-fold symmetry are common as icosahedra
Any rotational symmetry is compatible with translational periodicity, so crystals with 7- or 8-fold axes can exist in principle
Only 1-, 2-, 3-, 4- and 6-fold axes are compatible with periodicity; quasicrystals showing 5-fold diffraction are not periodic
crystal-024.explanation: After a lattice is rotated about a rotation axis, the vectors joining lattice points must still be lattice translation vectors. This condition limits the rotation angle θ to values for which 2cosθ is an integer, so only 1-, 2-, 3-, 4- and 6-fold axes are allowed (the crystallographic restriction). For the same reason that regular pentagons cannot tile a plane without gaps, no periodic crystal has a 5-fold axis or one of 7-fold or higher. Yet materials whose sharp diffraction spots are arranged with 5-fold symmetry were found, for example in rapidly quenched Al–Mn alloys. These are quasicrystals: their atoms are arranged in an ordered way, but without translational periodicity.

crystal-025.question: Si (lattice parameter 0.5431 nm) and Ge (0.5658 nm) both have the diamond structure and form solid solutions at all compositions. If the lattice parameter varies linearly with composition (Vegard's law), which is closest to the lattice mismatch of Si₀.₈Ge₀.₂ relative to Si (the fractional difference in lattice parameter)?
crystal-025.explanation: Vegard's law gives a = 0.8 × 0.5431 + 0.2 × 0.5658 ≈ 0.5476 nm, so the fractional difference from Si is (0.5476 − 0.5431)/0.5431 ≈ 0.0084, about 0.84%. This is 0.2 times the mismatch between pure Ge and Si, (0.5658 − 0.5431)/0.5431 ≈ 4.2%. About 4.2% compares pure Ge with Si, ignoring the Ge fraction, and about 3.3% mistakes the Si fraction of 0.8 for the Ge fraction. Vegard's law is an approximation that treats the lattice expansion from solute atoms as additive, and real solid solutions can deviate slightly from a straight line. Even so, it is widely used to estimate the composition of a solid solution from a lattice parameter measured by XRD.
